# What Nextflow is {#sec-overview .unnumbered}

Nextflow runs workflows, which it calls pipelines, written in its own language,
built on Groovy. A pipeline is a set of processes connected by channels: the
input files go into a channel, each process takes values from its input
channels and runs a task for each, and its outputs go into new channels, which
feed the next processes. Values flow forward, and a task runs as soon as its
inputs have arrived. Every task runs in a directory of its own under `work/`,
from which the results are published. Almost everything that surprises
newcomers follows from the channels and from these directories: samples paired
with the wrong data, a process that runs once instead of a hundred times, and
results that vanish with the work directory (@sec-model). Working with Nextflow
comes down to writing processes and the workflow that connects them,
configuring where they run, running and resuming, and reading the directory of
a task that failed (@sec-usage).

[](index.qmd) explains what Nextflow shares with Snakemake and states the rules
for both. Many standard analyses, above all in genomics, exist as nf-core
pipelines, which are run rather than written (@sec-nf-core).

Since version 26.04, Nextflow reads every pipeline in its strict syntax, which
this document uses. A pipeline written for an older version may need
`NXF_SYNTAX_PARSER=v1`, or better, the version of Nextflow it was written for
([](index.qmd#sec-pin-manager)).

Checked against Nextflow 26.10.3.


# How Nextflow thinks {#sec-model}

A pipeline is a chain of channels and processes. A channel holds values, here
pairs of the code of a station and a file; a process runs one task per value;
and the outputs of its tasks go into the next channel in the order the tasks
end:

```default
channel   [007, raw/007.csv]   [012, raw/012.csv]   [031, raw/031.csv]
              |
process   CLEAN: one task per value, each in a directory work/<hash>/
              |
channel   [031, 031.parquet]   [007, 007.parquet]   [012, 012.parquet]
              |
process   FIT: one task per value
              |
channel   [012, 012.fit.parquet]   [031, 031.fit.parquet]   [007, ...]
              |   collect: all values into one list
process   SUMMARIZE: one task for all stations
              |
publish   results/summary.parquet
```


## Processes, channels, and tasks {#sec-dataflow}

A process is a step: what it takes, under `input:`, what it gives, under
`output:`, and a script that makes the one from the other, with directives such
as `cpus` and `container` (@sec-pipeline). A task is one run of a process, on
one set of input values. A channel is a queue of values, such as files or
tuples of an ID and its files, which a process or a factory, such as
`channel.fromPath`, fills and another process takes from. Operators make new
channels from old ones: `map` changes each value, `join` pairs the values of
two channels by their key, and `collect` gathers all values into one list. The
`workflow` block connects the channels and the processes, calling processes
like functions.

Nothing in the workflow says when a task runs. A process runs a task whenever
each of its input channels has a value for it, so the tasks of many processes
and stations run at the same time, as far as the executor allows. The
`workflow` block is not a script whose lines run one after the other on the
data; it sets up the connections, once, and the values then flow through them.


## Match by key, not by order {#sec-identity}

The tasks of a process end in any order, and their outputs enter the channel in
the order they end. Two channels that come from different processes therefore
hold their stations in different orders, and in other orders in every run. A
process with two input channels takes the next value from each: given the
cleaned data of the stations from one channel and their calibrations from
another, it calibrates station 012 with the values of 007, and the results look
like any other ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-loud)).

Carry the identity with the data. Make every value a tuple of an ID and its
files, such as `[id, file]`, and combine two channels with `join`, which pairs
the values with the same ID, into one input of the process. Even within one
channel the order changes from run to run: `collect` gathers the values in the
order the tasks ended, so a step that needs them in order sorts them itself,
such as by station.


## A queue is used up, a value is not {#sec-value}

A channel is of one of two kinds. A queue channel, such as one made by
`channel.fromPath`, hands out each of its values once, and a process with two
queue channels as inputs runs as many tasks as the shorter one has values. A
value channel holds one value, which every task reads. A file that every task
needs, such as a reference or a table of constants, belongs in a value channel:
given as a queue, with `channel.fromPath(params.reference)`, it pairs with the
first station only, the process runs one task instead of a hundred, and the
pipeline ends with success.

Pass such a file to the process directly, such as
`CLEAN(stations, params.reference)`, which wraps it in a value channel, or make
one with `channel.value`. The outputs of a process whose inputs are all values
are values too, so an index built once from a reference reaches every task.


## Every task runs in a directory of its own {#sec-workdir}

Each task gets a directory under `work/`, named after its hash, such as
`work/4f/9fdbb999c3a4e9e93932683fefa53a`. Nextflow links the input files of the
task into it, under their own names, writes the script with its values filled
in, and runs it there; afterwards, it takes the files that the outputs declare
from it. The directory keeps everything about the task:

| File | Holds |
|----------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `.command.sh` | The script as it ran, with its values filled in |
| `.command.run` | The wrapper that sets up the environment, such as the container, and runs `.command.sh` |
| `.command.out`, `.command.err` | The standard output and the standard error of the script |
| `.command.log` | Both together, as the executor saw them |
| `.exitcode` | The exit status of the script |

A script finds its inputs by name in its current directory, and should read and
write nowhere else. A path that the script reaches on its own, such as
`/project/reference/stations.csv`, works on the machine it was written on, but
it is no input of the task: Nextflow neither includes it in the hash
(@sec-resume) nor makes it available in a container or on a machine in the
cloud. A file that the script writes but no output declares stays in the
directory of the task and goes nowhere.


## Results are published as links {#sec-publish}

The outputs of the tasks stay in their directories. The workflow names those
worth keeping in its `publish:` section, and the `output` block says where in
the output directory, `results/` by default, each goes (@sec-pipeline). Unless
told otherwise, Nextflow publishes a file as a symbolic link into the work
directory, not as a copy. The results then look complete, but vanish when the
work directory is cleaned up, and a copy of `results/`, such as with `cp -r` or
`rsync -a`, holds only links. Publish copies, with
`workflow.output.mode = 'copy'` (@sec-config). Older pipelines, among them many
of nf-core, publish with the directive `publishDir` of each process instead,
whose `mode` has the same default.


## `-resume` reuses tasks by their hash {#sec-resume}

Every task gets a hash, computed from the name of its process, its script with
the values filled in, its input values and files, its container or Conda
environment, and the scripts of `bin/` that it calls. Nextflow keeps the hashes
in `.nextflow/cache`, and with `-resume`, it reuses each task whose hash it
finds and whose outputs are still in its directory, instead of running it.
Without `-resume`, it runs every task again, in new directories.

A file counts by its path, its size, and its time of last modification, not by
its contents: touching an input runs its tasks again, and so does a copy of the
inputs that renews their times. On a shared file system that reports the times
inconsistently, `cache = 'lenient'` in the `process` scope of the configuration
leaves the time out, and `cache = 'deep'` hashes the contents, which is
reliable and slow for large files. A change outside the task, such as a newer
package in an environment that is not pinned or a file that the script reads
from a path of its own (@sec-workdir), changes no hash and runs nothing again.


# Working with Nextflow {#sec-usage}

The examples are a pipeline that cleans the measurements of each station, fits
a model to each, and summarizes the fits. A package does the science, with a
command for each step, `stationfit clean`, `fit`, and `summarize`, installed in
a container image ([](index.qmd#sec-thin)).


## Write a pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

```groovy
// main.nf
params {
    input: String = 'data/raw/*.csv'
    seed: Integer = 42
}

process CLEAN {
    tag "${id}"
    container 'ghcr.io/lab/stationfit@sha256:<digest>'

    input:
    tuple val(id), path(raw)

    output:
    tuple val(id), path("${id}.parquet")

    script:
    """
    stationfit clean ${raw} --output ${id}.parquet
    """
}

process FIT {
    tag "${id}"
    container 'ghcr.io/lab/stationfit@sha256:<digest>'
    cpus 4
    memory 8.GB
    time 1.h

    input:
    tuple val(id), path(clean)
    val seed

    output:
    tuple val(id), path("${id}.fit.parquet")

    script:
    """
    stationfit fit ${clean} --output ${id}.fit.parquet \\
        --seed ${seed} --threads ${task.cpus}
    """
}

process SUMMARIZE {
    container 'ghcr.io/lab/stationfit@sha256:<digest>'

    input:
    path fits

    output:
    path 'summary.parquet'

    script:
    """
    stationfit summarize ${fits} --output summary.parquet
    """
}

workflow {
    main:
    raw = channel.fromPath(params.input).map { f -> tuple(f.baseName, f) }
    cleaned = CLEAN(raw)
    fits = FIT(cleaned, params.seed)
    summary = SUMMARIZE(fits.map { id, f -> f }.collect())

    publish:
    fits = fits
    summary = summary
}

output {
    fits {
        path 'fits'
    }
    summary {
        path '.'
    }
}
```

An input is a `val`, a value, or a `path`, a file that Nextflow links into the
directory of the task; a `tuple` keeps the code of a station together with its
file (@sec-identity). `tag` names each task in the progress of Nextflow, such as
`FIT (007)`. In the script, `${...}` inserts a value, and `task.cpus` the
number of CPUs of the task; a `$` meant for the shell is written `\$`, as in
`\$HOME`, and a backslash at the end of a line `\\`. The seed reaches `FIT` as a
plain value, which every task reads (@sec-value), and `collect` gathers the
fits into one list for one task of `SUMMARIZE`.

The `params` block declares the parameters with their types and defaults, and
`--seed 7` on the command line overrides one. With the block, a misspelled
parameter, such as `--sed 7`, or a value of the wrong type stops the run;
without it, Nextflow accepts both without a word, and every value from the
command line is text ([](index.qmd#sec-pin-manager)). A larger pipeline puts
its processes into modules, files that the workflow includes, such as with
`include { FIT } from './modules/fit'`.


## Configure it {#sec-config}

```groovy
// nextflow.config
manifest {
    nextflowVersion = '!>=26.04'
}

workflow.output.mode = 'copy'

process {
    shell = ['/bin/bash', '-euo', 'pipefail']
    cpus = 1
    memory = 2.GB
    time = 1.h
}

profiles {
    local {
        docker.enabled = true
    }
    slurm {
        process.executor = 'slurm'
        process.queue = 'cpu'
        executor.account = 'ocean-lab'
        executor.queueSize = 50
        apptainer.enabled = true
        apptainer.cacheDir = '/scratch/ocean-lab/apptainer'
    }
    test {
        params.input = 'tests/data/*.csv'
    }
}
```

Nextflow reads `nextflow.config` beside the pipeline and in the directory it is
started from, and a file given with `-c` overrides both. The `process` scope
sets defaults for every process, which the directives of a process override.
Two settings belong in every configuration. `pipefail` makes a task fail
whose pipe fails halfway, such as `stationfit fit … | gzip`: by default,
Nextflow runs scripts with `/bin/bash -ue`, which reports only the exit status
of the last command of a pipe
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-all-or-nothing)). And
`workflow.output.mode = 'copy'` publishes copies instead of links
(@sec-publish). `manifest.nextflowVersion` with `!` stops the run under any
version older than 26.04.

A profile collects the settings for one place ([](index.qmd#sec-profiles)), and
`-profile slurm,test` combines two. With `process.executor = 'slurm'`, every
task becomes a Slurm job in the partition `process.queue`, charged to
`executor.account`, and `executor.queueSize` limits how many of them wait or
run at once, 100 by default. With `apptainer.enabled`, Nextflow runs each task
in its image with Apptainer, after converting the image from its registry into
a SIF file in `apptainer.cacheDir`; `apptainer.runOptions` passes options to
it, such as those of [](../containers/apptainer.qmd#sec-host). nf-test runs a
pipeline or a single process on small inputs and checks its outputs, as nf-core
does for all of its pipelines and modules.


## Run, resume, and clean up {#sec-run}

```bash
nextflow run main.nf -profile slurm --seed 42 -with-report -with-trace
nextflow run main.nf -profile slurm --seed 42 -resume  # reuse the unchanged
nextflow log                                  # the runs, by name
nextflow log nostalgic_miescher -f name,status,workdir  # the tasks of one
nextflow clean -n -before nostalgic_miescher  # what cleaning would remove
nextflow clean -f -before nostalgic_miescher  # remove it
```

The options of Nextflow take one dash, such as `-resume` and `-profile`, and
the parameters of the pipeline two, such as `--seed`. A pipeline without a
`params` block takes `--resume`, with two dashes, for a parameter named
`resume`, and runs everything again. Every run gets a name, such as
`nostalgic_miescher`, by which `nextflow log` lists its tasks and
`-resume nostalgic_miescher` resumes it instead of the last run. `-with-report`
and `-with-trace` write a report and a table of every task, with its hash,
status, duration, and the memory and CPU it used
([](index.qmd#sec-records)).

`nextflow clean` removes the directories of the tasks of earlier runs, which
then can no longer be resumed; results published as links would point nowhere
(@sec-publish). On a cluster, start Nextflow where it can run for as long as
the pipeline ([](index.qmd#sec-executor)).


## When a task fails {#sec-debug}

```bash
cd work/e5/4067ac14ea8daf6602bb1ade80059d  # the directory from the error
cat .command.sh                            # the script as it ran
cat .command.err                           # what it wrote to standard error
bash .command.run                          # run it again, in its container
```

When a task fails, Nextflow stops the pipeline and prints the process, the exit
status, the end of the standard error, and the directory of the task. There,
`.command.sh` shows what ran, with the values filled in, and
`bash .command.run` runs it again as Nextflow did, so that a fix can be tried
before the pipeline is resumed.

```groovy
process FIT {
    errorStrategy { task.exitStatus in 137..140 ? 'retry' : 'terminate' }
    maxRetries 2
    memory { 8.GB * task.attempt }
    // ...
}
```

A task killed for its memory or its time, which ends with an exit status from
137 to 140, may succeed with more. Here, `FIT` asks for 8 GB more in each
attempt, `task.attempt`, and `errorStrategy` retries only such failures, so that
a defect still fails at once. `process.resourceLimits` in the configuration,
such as `[cpus: 32, memory: 256.GB, time: 48.h]`, caps every request at what
the cluster offers.


## Run an nf-core pipeline {#sec-nf-core}

```bash
nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq -r 3.27.0 -profile test,apptainer --outdir results
nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq -r 3.27.0 -profile apptainer \
    -params-file params.yaml -c cluster.config
```

nf-core pipelines are maintained by a community, with tests, releases, and the
documentation of every parameter on [nf-co.re](https://nf-co.re).
`nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq` downloads the pipeline from GitHub into
`~/.nextflow/assets`, and `-r` chooses the release
([](index.qmd#sec-pin-manager)). Every pipeline has a profile `test`, which
runs it on a small dataset and shows in minutes whether it works where it
should, and profiles for containers, such as `apptainer` and `docker`. Put the
parameters into a file, given with `-params-file`, which is kept with the
results, rather than on the command line, and the settings of the cluster into
a configuration given with `-c`; for many clusters, nf-core/configs already
holds one, used by its name as a profile.
